Summary

  1. SphereCeti: Trying a Tau Ceti-like approach to use agents to produce a decent-quality autoformalisation sitting on top of our current main
  2. Not a substitute for hand-formalisation, we can decide what to do with the code once it's written (use it/consult it/disregard it)
  3. Development on main continues in the meantime (there are many virtues to hand-formalisation and we don't want to disregard it entirely - I'll admit I lost motivation for a while, but it's coming back, and I really think a high-quality artefact would be valuable and lead to a lot of insight)
A message was moved here from #Sphere packing in 8 dimensions > Weekly Packathons @ CMU by Sidharth Hariharan.

I've made an initial roadmap PR at SphereCeti#1. Feel free to push commits directly to its branch or whatever is simplest for review. I don't have a strong opinion about any of the particular choices, but hopefully this will get us started.

Also feel free to change how it does CI or other repo setup.

The two most interesting bits of content are:

  • README.md
  • Suggested.lean

Other files of interest:

  • UPSTREAM.md
  • Pinned.lean
  • CONVENTIONS.md
  • MIGRATION.md

Done!
I've added a contour integral layer in 6060a6d and subsequent commits, and also addressed the various comments from earlier today.

I've added a stack of SphereCeti infrastructure PRs (adapting ideas and tools from TauCeti to our monorepo setting), along with a guide to them at SphereCeti#23.

Could someone (e.g., @Chris Birkbeck) please take a look when you have a chance?

I'd suggest starting with SphereCeti#4 → SphereCeti#5 → SphereCeti#6 → SphereCeti#8.

(The roadmap PR SphereCeti#1 is unchanged.)
This looks great! I think we can just approve them all, so I approved 4,5,6,8. If you tell me what order the others should go in I'll do those as well

Thanks, I just merged 4, 5, 6, 8 into main as one stack, and am currently republishing the remaining stack, keeping the roadmap PR SphereCeti#1 on top.

Originally I had prioritized having more leaves independently reviewable, but this new stack will be prioritizing ease of review in one sequence:

main, 9, 10, 11, 19, 21, 22, 20, 24, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 18, 17, 1

I'll write again here when it's ready.
The rearrangement is complete -- see SphereCeti#23 for a guide.

OK I skimmed the infrastructure PRs and it all looks good to me, I'm not really an expert but it all looked sensible so I just approved them. Will do one more pass on the roadmap and then hopefuly thats good to go

Thanks. I've just merged the portion of the stack that was ready (9 -> ... -> 15), but beyond those 12 PRs there's something in 16 and 18 blocking 17. Not sure if it's just waiting for CI, or needs a review, or needs something to be fixed, but I'll look into it.
@Chris Birkbeck I was able to merge 16 after CI passed again, but I think gh now requires your approval again for 18 and 17. After that it'll be just the roadmap PR.
FYI Fourier interpolation in 8 and 24 dimensions has been solved on LeanEval recently, though no solution is public.
That's interesting, I didn't even know that the statement was on LeanEval.
Same here! Very cool

Kim Morrison (using Codex) originally opened https://github.com/leanprover/lean-eval/pull/494 to add interpolation on the real line (only uniqueness, no existence), but I noted that the 8 & 24-dim results (existence & uniqueness) are also easy (even easier) to state, so the 8 & 24-dim results end up being merged and not the 1-dim one ...

I think 1-dim case also should be doable assuming that we already have 8 and 24 (if you want to add it to LeanEval then I can take a look, but it should be quite easy to state). Also there are "two" proofs for the 1-dim case, (original) one by Radchenko--Viazovska and the other by Gerbelli-Gauthier--Venkatesh. Two proofs are completely different and it would be interesting to see formalize both of them.
Also I was a bit surprised that both 8 and 24 interpolation formula are formalized, until I realize that it doesn't mean that universal optimality of the lattices are also done (which should be doable, but it includes heavy numerical calculations and proof would be messy).

Thanks for the references! I didn't read the interpolation paper carefully enough to notice what the gap between interpolation and universal optimality is, and I'm surprised to learn it's heavily numerical. The 1-dim statement is in this comment but Kim didn't take it in the end.

theorem radchenko_viazovska_interpolation :
    ∃ e : {f : 𝓢(ℝ, ℂ) // Function.Even f} ≃
      {a : Set.Ici 0 × Fin 2 → ℂ //
        tsum (fun k : ℤ ↦ a (⟨k.natAbs ^ 2, by simp⟩, 0)) =
        tsum (fun k : ℤ ↦ a (⟨k.natAbs ^ 2, by simp⟩, 1)) ∧
        ∀ j, RapidlyDecreasing fun k ↦ a (k, j)},
    ∀ f, (e f).1 = Function.uncurry fun k ↦ ![f.1 √k.1, 𝓕 f.1 √k.1] := by
  sorry
I think you need to take a subspace of RHS given by poisson summation formula.

The tsum = tsum condition is exactly to cut out this subspace ...

I think 1-dim case also should be doable assuming that we already have 8 and 24 (if you want to add it to LeanEval then I can take a look

If the 1-dim proof is easier than 8 & 24-dim then it might no longer serve as a good eval problem now that 8 & 24-dim are solved. However, it appears that this first order interpolation (at N\sqrt{\mathbb{N}}N​) result has since been generalized to arbitrary dimensions; this is stated as (1.1) in https://arxiv.org/html/2510.04873v2 and supposedly and easy corollary of Theorem 3.1 of https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.02996. AI is telling me that there are ⌊d/4⌋+1 relations in dimension d (not necessarily just the one from Poisson summation, the number is the dimension of a certain space of modular forms), which I'm not sure are gonna be easy to write down ...

The tsum = tsum condition is exactly to cut out this subspace ...

Oops my bad! You are completely right.

I think the paper you mentioned (Radchenko-Sun) might be a good problem. To be honest I only care about actual solutions of LeanEval submissions (not the fact that something got solved), and especially any solution for the dimension 3, 4 interpolation formula would have some definition of Maass wave forms and Kloosterman sums (or at least something related to them), which are the actual valuable outcomes. Probably more challenging problem is to prove explicit formula of basis functions.

But if they solve dim 3,4 via the arbitrary dimension result (BRS, 2005.02996) then they wouldn't need to introduce Maass wave forms and Kloosterman sums? Two submissions for dim 8 & 24 have planned publication date 2026-10-30 and 2026-11-12, but apparently one team hasn't published a solution that was due on 2026-08-31 ...

If problem only asks to prove existence of interpolation basis, then I think BRS is enough and formalizing BRS might be harder than RV but not too much (I only skimmed through BRS, but the idea/materials used there seems quite close to RV). So I think one should ask to prove explicit formula for the bases in case of RS (d=3,4). Probably one can be more challenging by asking to prove all of Theorem 1.3 of RS, which needs Kloosterman sum bound, which needs Weil...

Yeah Kloosterman sum bound is one of the things left out in https://github.com/openai/primegaps186 ...
but we already have Weil conjectures and Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture in LeanEval ...

Yeah I also agree that is it not a good idea to add another question on Weil (and I'm the one who added Ramanujan-Petersson). But I think asking for explicit bases in case of dimension 3 and 4 is still a nice problem - so it would be Theorem 1.2(1) and Theorem 1.3(1) of RS, which would naturally include Theorem 1.1 too.

The "informal proof" of Ramanujan-Petersson is inaccurate I think: the eigenvalues of the weight k form show up not in the etale cohomology of the universal curve but in its (k-2)th fibre power E×SE×S…E \times_S E \times_S \ldotsE×S​E×S​…. For example the eigenvalues of weight 2 forms don't show up in the cohomology of the universal curve but in the cohomology of the base (the modular curve)

This is what Freitag--Kiehl says about the proof


so if we use the generalized Weil conjecture that applies to the derived pushforward of a constant sheaf, we can avoid taking the fibre power.
Yes, but then you're taking the cohomology of the base, not the elliptic curve, so again the informal proof is incorrect.

Yeah I agree now, it appears that "the étale cohomology of the universal elliptic curve over the modular curve" is intended to mean "universal curve over the modular curve" and not "cohomology over the modular curve". Also the reference is to Weil I (1974) rather than Weil II (1980). Likely Claude hallucinated a bit when preparing https://github.com/leanprover/lean-eval/pull/481
How should I change it then? I only checked the Lean statement carefully when I make the PR.
The conjecture about growth of tau is solely due to Ramanujan and should not have Petersson’s name attached.

1. Universal optimality of the triangular lattice. Proves that the triangular lattice minimizes the lower limit of energy per particle for every nonnegative completely monotone potential of squared distance among locally finite planar configurations of centered-disk density one. It also minimizes unit-background renormalized Riesz energies for 0 < 𝑠 < 2 and Coulomb energy, resolving Sandier–Serfaty and the two-dimensional Brauchart–Hardin–Saff conjecture on the linear term of optimal spherical log-arithmic energy.
    Atomic certificate · Universal optimality · Fourier circle-packing certificate · Coulomb renormalized energy

Looks like the 2-dim magic function has been constructed from https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/lean/docs/090.md

I saw that too! That one was actually first problem I searched when whole thing dropped. I will take a look soon, but the construction looks quite "non-magic" (messier than I thought). But it told me more interesting fact that someone already constructed a function in their Bachelor's(!) thesis, but the manuscript is not available publicly. It might be the case that two functions are different, since (if I understood correctly) magic function might not uniquely exist in dimension 2 (see here).
